outputs.L1: We introduce a new class of canonical analytic Zariski decompositions (AZDs), called supercanonical AZDs, on the canonical bundles of smooth projective varieties with pseudoeffective canonical classes. We investigate the variation of the supercanonical AZD \(\hat{h}_{\mathrm{can}}\) under projective deformations and provide a new proof of the invariance of plurigenera.
outputs.L2: We define a novel family of canonical analytic Zariski decompositions (AZDs), termed **supercanonical AZDs**, for the canonical bundles of smooth projective varieties whose canonical classes are pseudoeffective. We then examine how the supercanonical AZD \(\hat{h}_{can}\) behaves in projective families and use this analysis to derive an alternative proof of the invariance of plurigenera.
outputs.L3:
Supercanonical analytic Zariski decompositions (AZDs) form a new class of canonical singular Hermitian metrics associated with the canonical bundle of a smooth projective variety. When the canonical class is pseudoeffective—that is, when it lies in the closure of the cone of effective divisor classes—the canonical bundle admits a supercanonical AZD, denoted by \(\hat{h}_{can}\). This metric captures the positivity of the canonical bundle while encoding its unavoidable singularities, thereby providing an analytic counterpart to an algebraic Zariski decomposition.

A central feature of the construction is its behavior in projective families. Given a projective deformation of smooth projective varieties whose canonical classes are pseudoeffective, one studies how the corresponding metrics \(\hat{h}_{can}\) vary from fiber to fiber. The resulting control over their singularities and positivity makes it possible to compare pluricanonical sections across the family. In particular, this framework leads to a new analytic proof of the invariance of plurigenera: for every positive integer \(m\), the dimension
\[
P_m(X_t)=\dim H^0(X_t,mK_{X_t})
\]
remains constant under smooth projective deformations.
outputs.L4:
Let \(X\) be a smooth projective variety whose canonical bundle \(K_X\) is pseudoeffective. The work constructs a distinguished singular Hermitian metric on \(K_X\), called the supercanonical analytic Zariski decomposition (AZD). This metric has semipositive curvature in the sense of currents and captures the asymptotic behavior of all pluricanonical sections: its singularities do not eliminate any sections of \(mK_X\), so the spaces of global pluricanonical forms can be recovered using the associated multiplier ideal sheaves. Unlike constructions that depend on auxiliary choices, the supercanonical AZD is designed to be intrinsic and compatible with the birational geometry of \(X\).

The main issue is then to understand how these metrics behave in a projective family. Given a projective deformation \(f\colon \mathcal X\to S\) with smooth fibers, the supercanonical AZDs on the canonical bundles of the fibers can be related to a singular Hermitian metric on the relative canonical bundle \(K_{\mathcal X/S}\). Positivity results for relative canonical metrics, together with extension theorems for pluricanonical forms and careful control of multiplier ideals, show that the fiberwise metrics vary in a suitably semicontinuous manner. In particular, sections on an individual fiber can be extended to nearby fibers without losing control of their \(L^{2}\)-norms or their vanishing along the singularities of the metric.

These metric estimates lead to a new proof of the invariance of plurigenera. For every positive integer \(m\), the plurigenus
\[
P_m(X_s)=\dim H^0(X_s,mK_{X_s})
\]
is constant as \(s\) varies in a smooth projective family. The argument interprets pluricanonical sections through the supercanonical AZD and uses the positivity of the relative metric to obtain the required extension and comparison results. Thus, rather than treating invariance primarily as an algebraic statement about the direct images of pluricanonical bundles, the proof derives it from the geometry of canonical singular metrics.

The construction strengthens the role of analytic Zariski decompositions in deformation theory. It shows that canonical metrics not only encode the birational and asymptotic properties of a single variety, but also provide a natural mechanism for controlling those properties in families. In this way, the supercanonical AZD offers a unified analytic framework connecting pseudoeffectivity, pluricanonical systems, extension theory, and the deformation invariance of fundamental birational invariants.
outputs.L5:
## AZD: A Key Prefix in Pharmaceutical Research

AZD is commonly used as a development code for experimental medicines created by the pharmaceutical company AstraZeneca. During early research and clinical trials, new drug candidates are often identified by an AZD number before receiving a generic or commercial name.

A well-known example is **AZD1222**, the original development name for the Oxford–AstraZeneca COVID-19 vaccine. Other compounds include **AZD9291**, later approved as the cancer medicine osimertinib, and **AZD5363**, now known as capivasertib.

These codes allow researchers, regulators, and healthcare professionals to track a compound throughout laboratory studies and clinical development. An AZD designation does not necessarily mean that a medicine has been approved; many candidates remain under investigation or are discontinued if they do not meet safety and efficacy requirements.

Thus, AZD is closely associated with pharmaceutical innovation, particularly in areas such as oncology, respiratory disease, cardiovascular medicine, immunology, and vaccines.

counterfactuals.prompt: Describe how a new class of canonical analytic Zariski decompositions can yield another proof of the invariance of plurigenera.
counterfactuals.output:
Let \(f:X\to \Delta\) be a smooth projective family and \(X_t=f^{-1}(t)\). The goal is to show that
\[
P_m(X_t)=h^0(X_t,mK_{X_t})
\]
is independent of \(t\).

The argument uses a canonical analytic Zariski decomposition (AZD) of the canonical bundle, constructed from pluricanonical sections themselves. Schematically, one considers the fiberwise extremal functions
\[
B_{m,t}(x)=\sup\left\{|s(x)|^{2/m}:\ s\in H^0(X_t,mK_{X_t}),\ 
\int_{X_t}|s|^{2/m}\le 1\right\},
\]
and forms an upper-semicontinuous envelope of their asymptotic limit. Its reciprocal defines a singular Hermitian metric \(h_{\mathrm{can},t}\) on \(K_{X_t}\).

These metrics have three essential features:

1. **Semipositive curvature.**  
   The curvature current of \(h_{\mathrm{can},t}\) is nonnegative.

2. **AZD property.**  
   The metric loses no pluricanonical sections:
   \[
   H^0\!\left(X_t,mK_{X_t}\otimes
   \mathcal I(h_{\mathrm{can},t}^{\,m})\right)
   \simeq H^0(X_t,mK_{X_t}).
   \]
   Thus every pluricanonical section has precisely the integrability needed for \(L^2\)-extension arguments.

3. **Compatibility with families.**  
   The fiberwise constructions assemble into a relative singular metric
   \[
   h_{\mathrm{can}}\quad\text{on }K_{X/\Delta}
   \]
   with semipositive curvature. Positivity follows from the plurisubharmonic variation of the associated Bergman kernels, ultimately based on the Ohsawa–Takegoshi extension theorem. Its restriction to each fiber is an AZD with singularities comparable to the intrinsic canonical AZD of that fiber.

Now take \(s\in H^0(X_0,mK_{X_0})\). By the AZD property, \(s\) is integrable with respect to the appropriate power of \(h_{\mathrm{can}}|_{X_0}\). Applying the Ohsawa–Takegoshi theorem—after regularizing the metric if necessary—extends \(s\) to a section of \(mK_{X/\Delta}\) over a neighborhood of \(X_0\). Consequently, the restriction map
\[
H^0\!\left(f^{-1}(U),mK_{X/\Delta}\right)
   \longrightarrow H^0(X_0,mK_{X_0})
\]
is surjective.

A basis of \(H^0(X_0,mK_{X_0})\) therefore extends to nearby fibers and remains linearly independent after shrinking \(U\). Hence
\[
P_m(X_t)\ge P_m(X_0)
\]
for nearby \(t\). On the other hand, upper semicontinuity of cohomology gives
\[
P_m(X_t)\le P_m(X_0).
\]
Thus \(P_m(X_t)=P_m(X_0)\) locally, and therefore the plurigenera are constant throughout the family.

The advantage of these canonical AZDs is that, unlike an arbitrarily chosen AZD, they are defined intrinsically from pluricanonical sections and behave well under restriction to fibers. This makes the extension theorem directly applicable and yields a conceptually clean second proof of invariance of plurigenera.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4
